title: Sub-GHz Long Range (LoRa & LoRaWAN): Chirp Spread Spectrum, Spreading Factors & Link Budgets
goal: Transmit sensor telemetry over 15 kilometers on milliwatt battery power: master LoRa Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulation, Spreading Factors (SF7-SF12), regional 1% duty cycle laws, and LoRaWAN OTAA join handshakes.
recap: Yesterday we engineered high-bandwidth Wi-Fi and embedded TLS. Today we scale to extreme distances: engineering sub-GHz low-power wide-area networks (LPWAN) using LoRa and LoRaWAN.

parts.title: Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) Physics & Decoding Below Noise
say: Traditional radio modulations (FSK, PSK) encode data by shifting carrier frequency or phase. They require signals to be several decibels above the thermal noise floor to decode correctly.

LoRa (Long Range) uses Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS). The carrier frequency sweeps continuously across a calibrated bandwidth (typically 125 kHz or 250 kHz). An 'up-chirp' sweeps linearly from the lowest frequency to the highest; a 'down-chirp' sweeps in reverse.

Data symbols are encoded by cyclically shifting the starting frequency of each chirp. Because the receiver knows the exact mathematical slope of the chirp, it performs matched filtering (Fast Fourier Transform cross-correlation).

This gives LoRa extraordinary receiver sensitivity (-138 dBm to -142 dBm), enabling the radio to demodulate signals up to 20 dB BELOW the ambient thermal noise floor. A 25mW (+14 dBm) transmission can achieve a 15-kilometer link budget.
parts.example: A sensor buried in a concrete utility pit transmits at 868 MHz. Even though the received signal at the gateway is weaker than background cosmic and electrical noise, CSS cross-correlation reconstructs the packet flawlessly.

check.question: What allows LoRa Chirp Spread Spectrum signals to be demodulated even when received at power levels below the ambient thermal noise floor (-20 dB SNR)?
options: The receiver uses matched filter cross-correlation over the entire linear frequency chirp duration, concentrating spread signal energy while averaging out white noise.
The LoRa chip uses a quantum entanglement receiver.
The transmitter temporarily disables atmospheric radio noise.
LoRa only operates when the sun is down.
check.why: CSS spreads signal energy across a wide bandwidth over time. The receiver's correlator integrates this energy synchronously, boosting the correlated chirp signal above the random, uncorrelated background noise.

parts.title: Spreading Factors (SF7 to SF12) & Time-on-Air (ToA) Calculations
say: There is no free lunch in physics. The extreme range of higher Spreading Factors comes at a severe price: Time-on-Air (ToA) and battery consumption.
Each step increase in Spreading Factor (from SF7 to SF8, up to SF12) doubles the duration of every single symbol. This halves the effective bit rate.

A 20-byte payload transmitted at SF7 requires approximately 61 milliseconds of radio airtime. The exact same 20-byte payload transmitted at SF12 requires 1,482 milliseconds (1.48 seconds) of continuous radio transmission!
Because an active transmitter draws 25mA to 120mA, transmitting at SF12 consumes over 24 times more battery energy per packet than SF7.

Adaptive Data Rate (ADR): Production LoRaWAN networks dynamically command nodes close to the gateway to use SF7 to save battery, reserving SF12 exclusively for distant nodes at the edge of cell coverage.
parts.example: A smart water meter transmitting daily at SF7 consumes 0.0004 mAh per day; transmitting at SF12 consumes 0.01 mAh per day, reducing battery life from 15 years to 7 months.

check.question: Why is transmitting at LoRa Spreading Factor 12 (SF12) penalized by network operators and battery engineers?
options: SF12 increases Time-on-Air by > 20x compared to SF7, burning 20x more battery power and consuming shared RF channel capacity.
SF12 causes radio interference with commercial passenger aircraft.
SF12 can only be received by satellites in low Earth orbit.
SF12 transmits in plain text without AES encryption.
check.why: Higher spreading factors spread bits over longer chirp durations. At SF12, a small packet takes over 1.3 seconds of continuous transmission, occupying the RF channel for an extended period and rapidly draining battery reserves.

parts.title: Regional 1% Duty Cycle Invariant & Airtime Budget Trackers
say: Because LoRa operates in unlicensed ISM bands (such as 868 MHz in Europe and 915 MHz in the Americas), spectrum usage is strictly regulated by telecommunications authorities (ETSI, FCC).
In Europe (ETSI EN 300 220), the 868.0 to 868.6 MHz sub-band enforces a mandatory 1.0% Duty Cycle Limit.
The 1% Duty Cycle Invariant: Over any one-hour rolling window (3,600 seconds), a device is legally permitted to transmit for a maximum cumulative total of 36.0 seconds (1% of 3600s).
If a device transmits a packet at SF12 taking 1.48 seconds of airtime, it MUST enforce an immediate silent backoff delay of at least: T_off = (T_air / 0.01) - T_air = 99 * 1.48s = 146.5 seconds!
Firmware that violates the 1% duty cycle limit is illegal, risks heavy regulatory fines, jams the regional gateway, and fails carrier certification.
parts.example: Packet airtime = 0.5s. Minimum silent backoff before the radio is legally allowed to transmit again: 0.5s * 99 = 49.5 seconds.
parts.output:

codeNotes.note: In ETSI European regulations, 1% duty cycle restricts total transmission to 36 seconds per hour.
Formula T_off = T_air * 99 calculates the exact legal rest period required before the next transmission.
Persistent non-volatile budget tracking prevents radio abuse even across microcontroller reboots.

parts.tryIt: Calculate the backoff delay required after sending a 2-second packet in a 0.1% sub-band.

check.question: What is the legal consequence of the European 1% ISM band duty cycle rule for an IoT device transmitting a packet taking 1.0 second of airtime?
options: The device must remain completely silent for at least 99.0 seconds before transmitting on that sub-band again.
The device must pay a 1 euro tax per packet.
The device must switch to 5G cellular immediately.
The device must re-flash its bootloader.
check.why: A 1% duty cycle means the transmitter can only be active for 1/100th of total elapsed time. For every 1.0 second of transmission, the radio must remain silent for 99.0 seconds (1.0 / (1.0 + 99.0) = 1%).

parts.title: LoRaWAN MAC Classes & Over-The-Air Activation (OTAA)
say: LoRa is the physical RF modulation; LoRaWAN is the media access control (MAC) and network protocol linking nodes to cloud application servers.

LoRaWAN defines three device classes: Class A (Lowest power, bidirectional: each uplink is followed by two short downlink receive windows, RX1 and RX2; the device sleeps at all other times); Class B (Beacon-synchronized receive slots); Class C (Continuous listening, mains-powered, zero downlink latency).
Device Activation: ABP vs OTAA. In ABP (Activation By Personalization), encryption keys are hardcoded into Flash (insecure). Production systems mandate OTAA (Over-The-Air Activation).
OTAA Handshake: The node transmits an unencrypted Join-Request containing its DevEUI, JoinEUI (AppEUI), and DevNonce, signed with an AES-128 Message Integrity Code (MIC) using its secret root AppKey.

The network server responds with a Join-Accept. Both sides cryptographically derive two ephemeral session keys: NwkSKey (Network Session Key, encrypting MAC commands) and AppSKey (Application Session Key, encrypting user telemetry with AES-128 CTR).

Mitigating Join Storms: When a citywide power outage resolves, thousands of sensors reboot simultaneously. Nodes MUST implement randomized exponential backoff delays to prevent destructive Join-Request collisions on default channels.
parts.example: 500 streetlights reboot together. Without jitter, all 500 transmit Join-Requests at t=0, causing a 100% collision blackout. With randomized backoff, requests scatter across 0-60 seconds, achieving a 99% join success rate.
parts.output:
--- DAY 33 PART 4: LORAWAN OTAA JOIN HANDSHAKE ---
[LORAWAN-OTAA] Transmitting Join-Request (DevNonce: 1):

  DevEUI:  0x4a30b001f23a4
  JoinEUI: 0x70b3d57ed0001234
  -> Signed with AES-128 MIC using root AppKey.
[LORAWAN-OTAA] Received Join-Accept in RX1 Window!

codeNotes.note: OTAACredentials contains persistent root identity: 64-bit DevEUI, 64-bit JoinEUI, and 128-bit AppKey.
Randomized startup jitter delay (e.g. 2450ms) prevents join storms when power is restored across a region.
Join-Accept derives two distinct AES-128 session keys, isolating network routing security from application payload privacy.

parts.tryIt: Explain how DevNonce prevents replay attacks: why must a LoRaWAN network server reject Join-Requests with reused DevNonces?

check.question: What two distinct AES-128 session keys are cryptographically generated upon completing a LoRaWAN OTAA Join handshake?
options: NwkSKey (Network Session Key for MAC integrity) and AppSKey (Application Session Key for end-to-end payload encryption).
A Wi-Fi WPA2 password and an SSL certificate.
A Bluetooth pairing PIN and an RFID tag number.
A private RSA key and a public PGP key.
check.why: LoRaWAN decouples network operators from application data providers. The network server uses NwkSKey to validate MAC commands and check frame counters, while the application payload can only be decrypted by the final application server holding the AppSKey.

parts.title: Master Engine: LoRaWAN Class A Node & Link Budget Simulator
say: We now assemble the complete Day 33 Master Engine: an industrial LoRaWAN Class A transceiver platform.

Our engine models: 1) SX1262 SPI register driver simulation; 2) Spreading Factor selection and dynamic Time-on-Air calculation; 3) European 1% Duty Cycle legal enforcement; 4) OTAA Join request generation with randomized jitter; 5) Class A bidirectional communication opening synchronous RX1 and RX2 receive windows.
This architecture represents the exact embedded firmware required to deploy smart agricultural monitors, pipeline leak detectors, and long-range municipal utility meters.
parts.example: Executing the engine demonstrates an OTAA join, payload airtime calculation, duty cycle compliance, and dual receive window listening with zero regulatory violations.

check.question: In a LoRaWAN Class A device, when is the node's radio receiver enabled to listen for downlink messages from the cloud?
options: Exclusively during two short receive windows (RX1 and RX2) scheduled at fixed intervals (e.g. 1s and 2s) immediately following an uplink transmission.
Continuously 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Only on Sunday mornings.
Whenever the temperature drops below zero.
check.why: Class A devices are optimized for maximum battery life. The radio receiver is powered off 99.9% of the time, opening two brief receive windows (RX1 and RX2) exclusively after the node transmits an uplink message.

summary: LoRa uses Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) to demodulate signals up to 20 dB below thermal noise with -138 dBm sensitivity.
Spreading Factors (SF7 to SF12) double symbol duration at each step; SF12 covers extreme range but takes 20x longer airtime and 20x more battery energy.
Regional regulations mandate a 1% Duty Cycle Limit (maximum 36 seconds of airtime per hour), requiring mandatory silent backoff delays.
LoRaWAN Class A nodes open two receive windows (RX1 and RX2) only after transmitting an uplink, sleeping at under 2 microamps at all other times.
OTAA activation securely derives NwkSKey and AppSKey session keys; randomized startup jitter is required to prevent join storms after power outages.

steps: Initialize the SPI bus interface connected to the Semtech SX1262 / SX1276 transceiver.
Load DevEUI, JoinEUI, and root AppKey into secure hardware storage.
